newsitem.title: JAPAN: FOCUS -- Weak Tokyo stocks hurt second-tier brokers.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS -- Weak Tokyo stocks hurt second-tier brokers.

text.p: Almost all of Japan's second-tier securities houses said on Thursday that they had posted parent current losses for the business year ended March 31, but many of them expected profits in the current 1997/98 year.
Nine out of the 10 second-tier brokerages said that lower stock prices in 1996/97 were a major reason why they were forced to post losses due to appraisal losses on their shareholdings.
Some also said that their stock brokering businesses were hurt by the fact that many individual investors chose to stay out of the sluggish Tokyo stock market.
Japan's "Top Four" brokers and another second-tier broker Kokusai Securities Co Ltd last month announced parent current profits for 1996/97.

The daily average turnover at the Tokyo Stock Exchange was up 0.6 percent from a year earlier to about 399 billion yen in 1996/97, but the increase in the volume reflected active participation by foreign investors who bought shares mainly through foreign brokerages, the brokers added.

The nine are Kankaku Securities Co Ltd, Sanyo Securities Co Ltd, New Japan Securities Co Ltd, Cosmo Securities Co Ltd, Yamatane Securities Co Ltd, Okasan Securities Co Ltd, Wako Securities Co Ltd, Dai-Ichi Securities Co Ltd and Tokyo Securities Co Ltd.
Parent current losses at the nine firms ranged from Okasan's 1.72 billion yen to Kankaku's 21.42 billion yen.

A Kankaku executive told reporters the brokerage, which is more dependent on income from stock brokering fees than other second-tier brokerages, suffered a nearly 20 percent year-on-year decline in fee income.
The decline was mainly due to the foreign brokerages' success in capturing a larger share of the business, he said.

Meanwhile, all of the nine second-tier brokerages except for Tokyo Securities said that they expect total parent current profits to range from 385 billion yen to 450 billion yen in the 1997/98 year based on the TSE's daily average volume.
Tokyo Securities said that it had decided not to announce its earnings forecast from the current business year and would unveil its earnings on a quarterly basis.
Of the nine, Sanyo and Wako have been providing financial support to their financial affiliates.

A Sanyo executive said that the broker held some 80 billion yen worth of its affiliates' problem loans but offered no financial assistance to the four affiliates in 1996/97 as the parent company itself posted losses.

He also said the brokerage had provided 8.3 billion yen worth of financial assistance to the affiliates over the past three years, which was much smaller than the 45 billion yen it had originally planned.
In order to restructure its business, Sanyo will close subsidiaries in New York and Geneva and representative offices in Beijing and Seoul in 1997/98, he said.

Asked how it will cope with the expected liberalisation of stock brokering fees, an executive at Yamatane Securities said that the company would pay more attention to its asset management business for individuals.
"Not only for us, but also for other brokers, it is not an easy task to weather (financial deregulation). But we must do it," he said.
